lessons.title: Overview of Roofing Sheets in Construction
lessons.body:
Roofing sheets are flat, thin panels made from materials like galvanized steel, aluminium, or plastic. They are used to cover buildings and protect people and goods from rain, sun, and wind. In Africa, the most common roofing sheet is corrugated galvanized iron (CGI), often called 'mabati' in East Africa or 'zinc' in West Africa. A standard sheet is about 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm thick, 762 mm or 900 mm wide, and can be cut to any length. The wavy corrugations give strength and allow sheets to overlap so water runs off.

Roofing sheets are popular because they are cheap, light, and quick to install. A 3-metre sheet of 0.3 mm CGI costs about $10 to $15 in many African markets. One worker can carry and fix them without heavy machinery. They are used on homes, shops, schools, clinics, and warehouses. Unlike thatch or mud, they do not rot or burn easily. However, they can be noisy in heavy rain and get very hot in direct sun unless insulated.

When choosing roofing sheets, consider the climate. In coastal areas like Mombasa or Lagos, salt in the air rusts ordinary steel quickly, so you need galvanized or aluminium sheets. In hot dry areas like northern Nigeria or the Sahel, heat reflection matters, so light-coloured or coated sheets work better. In rainy regions like the Congo Basin, use thicker sheets (0.4 mm or more) and steep slopes (at least 22 degrees) to shed water fast.

Roofing sheets are fixed to a timber or steel frame called trusses and purlins. The sheets overlap by at least one corrugation sideways and 150 mm end-to-end. Special nails or screws with rubber washers go through the crest (top of the wave) to prevent leaks. A typical 3-bedroom house needs about 40 to 60 sheets, depending on roof size and pitch. Proper installation means no leaks for 10 to 20 years, even in heavy tropical rain.

lessons.title: Historical Development of Roofing Materials
lessons.body:
Before roofing sheets, African builders used local materials: thatch from grass or palm fronds, mud, stone, and later baked clay tiles. Thatch was cheap and cool but needed replacing every 2 to 5 years and caught fire easily. Clay tiles lasted longer but were heavy and required skilled labour. In the 1800s, European traders brought corrugated iron sheets to coastal ports like Accra, Mombasa, and Cape Town. These sheets were light, strong, and fire-resistant, so they spread quickly along trade routes.

The first corrugated iron was made in Britain in the 1820s by rolling hot iron between grooved rollers. It was galvanized with zinc to stop rust. By the 1900s, steel replaced iron, and sheets became cheaper. In colonial Africa, railways and missions used CGI for warehouses, churches, and staff housing. After independence in the 1960s, local factories in Kenya, Nigeria, South Africa, and Egypt began producing sheets, cutting import costs.

In the 1960s and 70s, asbestos-cement sheets became common because they did not rust and were fireproof. But asbestos causes lung cancer, and by the 1990s most African countries banned it. Today, alternatives include fibre-cement, which uses cellulose and cement, and plastic sheets like polycarbonate. Aluminium sheets, popular in coastal areas, resist salt but cost more. Coated steel with zinc-aluminium alloy (like Zincalume) lasts up to 25 years.

Modern roofing sheets now come in many profiles: corrugated, trapezoidal, standing seam, and tile-effect. Some have insulation foam bonded to the back to reduce heat and noise. In Africa, the most common remains the simple corrugated galvanized sheet because it is affordable and available in every town. Understanding this history helps you choose the right sheet for your climate and budget, and appreciate why maintenance matters.

lessons.title: Types of Roofing Sheets: An Introduction
lessons.body:
There are five main types of roofing sheets you will see in Africa. First, corrugated galvanized iron (CGI): wavy sheets made of steel coated with zinc. They are the cheapest and most common. Thickness ranges from 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm. A 0.3 mm sheet lasts about 10 years in mild conditions, less near the coast. Second, aluminium sheets: lightweight, rust-proof, and good for coastal areas, but soft and more expensive. They are often used on hotels and high-end homes.

Third, coated steel sheets: steel with a layer of zinc-aluminium alloy plus a paint coating (e.g., red, green, blue). Brands like Dumuzas, Mabati, and Roofings make these. They last 15 to 25 years and come in tile profiles or trapezoidal shapes. They cost about 30% more than plain CGI but save on repainting. Fourth, fibre-cement sheets: made from cement, cellulose, and sand. They do not rust, are quiet in rain, and resist fire. But they are heavy and brittleâyou must drill holes before nailing. They are common in Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Fifth, plastic sheets: polycarbonate or PVC. They are transparent or translucent, letting light in. Used for skylights, greenhouses, and verandas. They are lightweight but expand in heat and can crack if not fixed with oversized holes. They cost about $15 per square metre. Also, there are bitumen sheets (roofing felt) for flat roofs, but they are not common in African pitched roofs.

When choosing, ask: What is my budget? How long do I want the roof to last? Is it near the sea? Will it be walked on? For a typical rural home, 0.3 mm CGI is fine. For a coastal hotel, use aluminium or coated steel. For a clinic that needs quiet, use fibre-cement. Always buy from a reputable dealer and check for the zinc coating weight (e.g., Z275 means 275 g/mÂ² of zinc).

lessons.title: Basic Terminology and Components
lessons.body:
To work with roofing sheets, you must know the parts. The sheet itself is the panel. Corrugation is the wavy shapeâcrest is the top of the wave, valley is the bottom. Pitch is the slope of the roof, measured in degrees. A low pitch (below 15Â°) needs more overlap and may leak; a steep pitch (above 30Â°) sheds water fast. Span is the distance between supports. Purlins are horizontal timber or steel bars that hold the sheets. Trusses are the triangular frames that support the purlins.

Other terms: Overlap is how much one sheet covers another. Side overlap is one corrugation (about 75 mm). End overlap is 150 mm for low pitch, 100 mm for steep. Ridge is the top edge where two roof slopes meet; a ridge cap covers it. Eaves are the lower edge that hangs over the wall. Fascia is the board at the eaves. Gutter collects rainwater from the eaves. Flashing is a strip that seals joints around chimneys, vents, or walls.

Fixings include roofing nails (umbrella head) or screws (hex head with rubber washer). Nails are cheaper but can loosen; screws hold better. You drive them through the crest, not the valley, to prevent water sitting around the hole. A typical nail is 75 mm long. Washers are neoprene or rubber. Purlins are spaced 600 mm to 900 mm apart for 0.3 mm sheets; closer for thinner sheets.

Tools you need: hammer, claw hammer, tape measure, chalk line, tin snips (for cutting sheets), power drill with hex driver, ladder, safety harness, gloves, and goggles. A nibbler or angle grinder can cut sheets but creates hot sparksâavoid near flammable materials. Always wear gloves when handling sheets; edges are sharp. A string line helps keep sheets straight. Knowing these terms helps you order materials correctly and talk to suppliers without confusion.

lessons.title: Role of Roofing Sheets in Building Envelope
lessons.body:
The building envelope is the outer shell that separates inside from outside: roof, walls, windows, and doors. The roof is the most critical part because it takes the brunt of rain, sun, and wind. In Africa, a well-installed roofing sheet keeps out tropical downpours (up to 200 mm in a day) and blocks intense solar radiation (up to 1000 W/mÂ²). Without a good roof, walls get damp, ceilings stain, and health suffers from mould and mosquitoes.

Roofing sheets also affect indoor temperature. Bare galvanized steel can reach 70Â°C in the sun, radiating heat down. That is why many African homes have a ceiling: it traps air and reduces heat. You can also use reflective coatings (white paint) or insulated sheets with foam backing. In hot climates, a ventilated roof spaceâwith vents at eaves and ridgeâlets hot air escape. In rainy areas, the roof must slope enough to shed water quickly; a 22Â° pitch is minimum for CGI.

Structurally, roofing sheets are light (about 4 kg/mÂ² for 0.3 mm CGI), so they do not need heavy foundations. But they must be fixed securely against wind uplift. In cyclone-prone areas like Mozambique or Madagascar, use screws with washers and fix at every second corrugation. The roof also supports solar panels, water tanks, or satellite dishesâso plan for extra load. A typical 3-bedroom house roof might weigh 500 kg for sheets plus 300 kg for timber.

Finally, the roof affects water collection. In dry areas, gutters and tanks capture rainwater from the roof. A 100 mÂ² roof in a region with 500 mm annual rainfall can collect 50,000 litres per yearâenough for a family. But avoid lead or asbestos sheets for drinking water. Use food-grade plastic or coated steel. Proper roofing sheets thus protect health, comfort, and water supply.

lessons.title: Safety Practices for Roofing Work
lessons.body:
Roofing is dangerous. Falls are the leading cause of death in construction. In Africa, many workers die each year from falling off roofs. Before you start, check the weather: never work on a wet or windy roof. Wind can lift a sheet and throw you off. Use a safety harness anchored to a strong point, and wear non-slip shoes. If you feel dizzy or tired, stop. A ladder must be tied off and extend 1 metre above the eaves. Never stand on the top three rungs.

When handling sheets, wear thick gloves. Cut edges are razor-sharp. Carry sheets on edge, not flat, to avoid bending. Two people should carry long sheets. When cutting with tin snips or grinder, wear goggles and a dust maskâmetal dust harms lungs. If using a grinder, be aware of sparks that can burn you or start fires. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Do not cut sheets over a power line. Also, check for overhead wires before raising sheets.

On the roof, use roof jacks or crawling boards to spread your weight. Never walk on the unsupported middle of a sheet. Step on purlins or use a plank. Fix sheets from the bottom up, so you are always working over secured area. Secure each sheet with at least four fixings before moving. If you must work near the edge, install a temporary guardrail. In hot sun, drink water every 20 minutes to avoid heat stroke. Wear a hat and long sleeves.

After work, clean up all offcuts and nailsâthey cause tetanus. Wash hands before eating. Store sheets flat and dry, away from children. Train all workers on first aid and emergency numbers. In many African countries, there are no strict safety laws on small sites, so you must protect yourself. A safe worker is a productive worker. Remember: no roof is worth your life.

quiz.q: What is the most common roofing sheet material used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Corrugated galvanized iron (CGI) is the cheapest and most widely available roofing sheet in Africa.

quiz.q: What is the typical thickness range for CGI roofing sheets?
quiz.explanation: CGI sheets commonly range from 0.2 mm to 0.5 mm thick.

quiz.q: Why are corrugations added to roofing sheets?
options: B) To add strength and allow overlapping
quiz.explanation: Corrugations increase stiffness and allow sheets to overlap for water runoff.

quiz.q: In coastal areas, which roofing sheet is best to resist salt corrosion?
quiz.explanation: Aluminium resists salt corrosion better than ordinary steel.

quiz.q: What is the minimum recommended roof pitch for CGI sheets in rainy areas?
quiz.explanation: A pitch of at least 22 degrees helps shed water quickly and prevent leaks.

quiz.q: How much side overlap is recommended for corrugated sheets?
quiz.explanation: Side overlap of one corrugation (about 75 mm) is standard.

quiz.q: What is the end overlap for roofing sheets on a low-pitch roof?
quiz.explanation: End overlap of 150 mm is used for low-pitch roofs to prevent water entry.

quiz.q: Where should roofing nails be driven?
quiz.explanation: Nails go through the crest so water does not pool around the hole.

quiz.q: What is a purlin?
options: A) A type of roofing sheet
B) A horizontal support for sheets
quiz.explanation: Purlins are horizontal bars that support the roofing sheets.

quiz.q: Which material was banned in many African countries due to health risks?
quiz.explanation: Asbestos causes lung cancer and was banned in many countries.

quiz.q: What does Z275 mean on a galvanized sheet?
quiz.explanation: Z275 indicates a zinc coating weight of 275 grams per square metre.

quiz.q: Which roofing sheet is transparent and used for skylights?
quiz.explanation: Polycarbonate sheets are transparent or translucent and used for skylights.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a ridge cap?
options: B) To cover the top joint of two roof slopes
quiz.explanation: A ridge cap covers the ridge where two roof slopes meet.

quiz.q: What is flashing used for?
options: A) To seal joints around chimneys or walls
quiz.explanation: Flashing seals joints around penetrations like chimneys or vents.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for purlins with 0.3 mm CGI sheets?
quiz.explanation: Purlins are typically spaced 600 mm to 900 mm apart for 0.3 mm sheets.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to cut roofing sheets?
quiz.explanation: Tin snips are used to cut thin roofing sheets.

quiz.q: What should you wear when handling roofing sheets?
quiz.explanation: Thick gloves protect hands from sharp edges.

quiz.q: What is the leading cause of death in roofing work?
quiz.explanation: Falls are the leading cause of death in construction, including roofing.

quiz.q: When should you never work on a roof?
options: B) On a wet or windy day
quiz.explanation: Wet or windy conditions increase the risk of slips and falls.

quiz.q: How far above the eaves should a ladder extend?
quiz.explanation: A ladder should extend at least 1 metre above the eaves for safe access.

quiz.q: What is the role of a ceiling in a building with roofing sheets?
options: B) To reduce heat and noise
quiz.explanation: A ceiling traps air and reduces heat and noise from the roof.

quiz.q: How much rainwater can a 100 mÂ² roof collect in a region with 500 mm annual rainfall?
quiz.explanation: 100 mÂ² Ã 0.5 m = 50 mÂ³ = 50,000 litres.

quiz.q: Which roofing sheet is quietest in heavy rain?
quiz.explanation: Fibre-cement sheets are denser and quieter than metal sheets.

quiz.q: What does a neoprene washer do?
quiz.explanation: Neoprene washers seal around nail or screw holes to prevent leaks.

quiz.q: Which roofing material was introduced by European traders in the 1800s?
quiz.explanation: Corrugated iron sheets were brought to Africa by European traders in the 1800s.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of coated steel sheets over plain CGI?
quiz.explanation: Coated steel sheets last longer (15-25 years) due to additional protective layers.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of roof ventilation?
quiz.explanation: Ventilation allows hot air to escape, reducing indoor temperature.

quiz.q: How should you carry a long roofing sheet?
quiz.explanation: Carrying on edge prevents bending and damage.

quiz.q: What should you do before raising sheets near power lines?
quiz.explanation: Always check for overhead wires to avoid electrocution.

quiz.q: What is the first thing to do if you feel dizzy while on a roof?
options: B) Stop and get down safely
D) Lie down on the roof
quiz.explanation: Dizziness can lead to falls; stop and descend safely immediately.
